Here's some really quick and overly-simplified instructions on how to get KVM running. This should be enough to get you rolling. So easy, even a Windows user can do it :P

This post assumes you have already installed CentOS 7 on your server. Minimal install is fine. It also assumes that your KVM machine is on a secure network. Security will not be covered.

You need a computer that supports Intel VT-x or AMD-V. There's a setting in your Motherboard BIOS or UEFI settings that enables or disables these technologies. It's usually labeled "Virtualization" or some derivative.

Disable firewalld
sudo systemctl stop firewalld
sudo systemctl disable firewalld

Install The KVM Things
sudo yum groupinstall "Virtualization Host"

Enable KVM on Startup
sudo systemctl enable libvirtd

Restart the computer to enable the KVM kernel modules
sudo systemctl reboot

That's about it on the server side. Time to install the management tools on your computer. The trick to this is virt-manager. It's a GUI management system similar to what vSphere Client is to VMWare ESXi. However, it's only available on linux. Search for virt-manager in your operating systems software manager.

We'll need to set up an ssh key authentication to the root user on the KVM server (yes, I know, not very secure, but it's the easiest way to get up and running.) Here's a good tutorial on how to set up SSH keys. https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/how-to-set-up-ssh-keys--2

From there, you can log into the server as root using virt-manager (log in as root using the CLI first so the trust is generated.) If you have ever used VMWare, this should pretty fimiliar to you.
